newsitem.title: EGYPT: Sudan says signing treaty with rebel groups.
newsitem.headline: Sudan says signing treaty with rebel groups.

text.p: A Sudanese minister said on Sunday his government would clinch on April 21 a peace treaty with several rebel groups fighting for an independent south and called on Egypt to witness the signing.

Cabinet Affairs Minister Salah-Eddin Mohamed Ahmed Karra told reporters at Cairo airport while he was en route to Khartoum the agreement aimed at maintaining the unity of Sudan and that it would provide an opportunity for his country and northern neighbour Egypt to bury the hatchet.

"The signing of the agreement will take place on April 21, and will end battles between the government and the rebels for at least four years ... we would welcome Egypt to witness the signing as it will be a chance to forget or at least freeze our differences and reaffirm the unity of Sudan," Karra said.
Relations between the two countries hit bottom in 1995 after Cairo said Khartoum was harbouring gunmen charged with trying to kill Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak in Ethiopia.

But despite poor ties with the Khartoum government, Mubarak has called for a Sudan which has full control over the mainly Christian and animist south. Analysts say concern over Egypt's share of Nile water has prompted its stand.

Karra said that his government would accept secession for the south -- which is the main demand of the Sudan People's Liberation Army (SPLA) fighting for almost 13 years -- if the people choose independence through a referendum but said his government could keep Sudan together with Egypt's help.
"We can't go on fighting in the south forever but we can, with Egypt's cooperation, keep Sudan united and make the people of the south choose to remain united," he said.

Egypt is home to many key members of the Sudanese opposition who hold regular contacts with Egyptian officials. On Sunday, Egyptian Foreign Minister Amr Moussa held talks with former prime minister and opposition leader Sadeq al-Mahdi in Cairo on the situation in Sudan.
Earlier this month Mahdi said that the rebel coalition would consider any option -- even secession -- to end the war in the south.
Sudan has been riven by civil war for almost 13 years, with the south fighting what it sees as domination by the Moslem Arabised north.

The mainstream SPLA headed by John Garang refuses to hold peace talks with the government but since 1992, several smaller and marginal factions have left the SPLA and joined ranks with the state. The SPLA also recently joined a coalition of northern opposition parties fighting the government in the east and south.
